```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load packages
library(nnet)
library(AER)
```

Recall that for the baseline category logit model,
we assume the following:

- $Y_i\in\{0,1,2,\dotsc,M\}$.
- For each $m\in\{1,2,\dotsc,M\}$,
$$
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i = m\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i = 0\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip} \text{.}
$$

Below are the results of a baseline category logit model.

```{r}
# Create data set from Table 8.17 on page 331 of Categorical Data Analysis,
# 3rd ed, by Alan Agresti. Published by Wiley.
length <- c(1.30,1.32,1.32,1.40,1.42,
            1.42,1.47,1.47,1.50,1.52,
            1.63,1.65,1.65,1.65,1.65,
            1.68,1.70,1.73,1.78,1.78,
            1.80,1.85,1.93,1.93,1.98,
            2.03,2.03,2.31,2.36,2.46,
            3.25,3.28,3.33,3.56,3.58,
            3.66,3.68,3.71,3.89,1.24,
            1.30,1.45,1.45,1.55,1.60,
            1.60,1.65,1.78,1.78,1.80,
            1.88,2.16,2.26,2.31,2.36,
            2.39,2.41,2.44,2.56,2.67,
            2.72,2.79,2.84)
choice <- c("invertebrates","fish","fish","fish","invertebrates",
            "fish","invertebrates","fish","invertebrates","invertebrates",
            "invertebrates","other","other","invertebrates","fish",
            "fish","invertebrates","other","fish","other",
            "fish","fish","invertebrates","fish","invertebrates",
            "fish","fish","fish","fish","fish",
            "other","other","fish","fish","fish",
            "fish","other","fish","fish","invertebrates",
            "invertebrates","invertebrates","other","invertebrates","invertebrates",
            "invertebrates","fish","invertebrates","other","invertebrates",
            "invertebrates","fish","fish","fish","fish",
            "fish","fish","fish","other","fish",
            "invertebrates","fish","fish")

# Shift length
length_2 <- length - 2

# Outcome
table(choice)

# Baseline category logit model
mod_01 <- multinom(formula = choice ~ length_2)
# summary(mod_01)

# P-values
coeftest(mod_01)
```

Below are the exponentiated coefficients.

```{r}
# Exponentiated coefficients
co <- exp(summary(mod_01)$coefficients)
co

# Probabilities for two-meter-long alligators
p_f <- 1 / (1 + co[1,1] + co[2,1])
p_i <- co[1,1] * p_f
p_o <- co[2,1] * p_f
```

The "participants" in this study were 63 alligators caught in Lake George, Florida.
The variables are as follows:

- The outcome was primary food choice,
with three levels: fish, invertebrates, and other.
- `length_2` denotes length in meters, minus 2.
So, a three-meter-long alligator would have a value of 1 for this variable.

Please answer the following questions.

## Problem 1

(1 point)
Which primary food choice is most likely among alligators that are two meters long?
Ignore statistical significance.
Select only one of the following options.


(a) Fish
(b) Invertebrates
(c) Other
(d) It's impossible to know from the information provided.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Fish.

The probability that a two-meter-long alligator primarily eats invertebrates
is 53% lower than the probability that it primarily eats fish.
The probability that a two-meter-long alligator primarily eats other food
is 69% lower than the probability that it primarily eats fish.
So, fish must be the most likely choice among two-meter-long alligators.

:::

## Problem 2

(1 point)
Which primary food choice is most likely among alligators that are three meters long?
Ignore statistical significance.
Select only one of the following options.


(a) Fish
(b) Invertebrates
(c) Other
(d) It's impossible to know from the information provided.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Fish.

The ratio of the probability that an alligator primarily eats invertebrates
to the probability that it primarily eats fish decreases
by 92% with each one-meter increase in length.
The ratio of the probability that an alligator primarily eats other food
to the probability that it primarily eats fish decreases
by 8% with each one-meter increase in length.
Since these ratios were already less than 1 for two-meter-long alligators,
and they are decreasing,
the ratios must be less than 1 for three-meter-long alligators.

:::

## Problem 3

For each of the following pairs,
select whether the difference is statistically significant,
not statistically significant,
or whether it's impossible to tell based on the results above.
Each is worth one point.

### Part (a)

The probability that a two-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat fish
and the probability that a two-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat invertebrates.


(i) Statistically significant.
(ii) Not statistically significant.
(iii) Impossible to tell from the results above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Statistically significant.

This is tested in the following line:
        
```
                           Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
invertebrates:(Intercept) -0.763870   0.386543 -1.9762 0.048137 * 
```

:::

### Part (b)

The odds that a three-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat invertebrates
and the odds that a two-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat invertebrates.


(i) Statistically significant.
(ii) Not statistically significant.
(iii) Impossible to tell from the results above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible to tell.

This analysis does not use odds.

Even if this analysis did use odds,
the fact that the coefficient for `invertebrates:length_2`
is significantly different from zero
doesn't imply that there is a statistically significant
difference between any two groups of alligators
of different lengths.
We don't know if there even were any alligators who were
two or three meters long.
        

:::
        
### Part (c)

The probability that a two-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat fish
and the probability that a two-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat other food.


(i) Statistically significant.
(ii) Not statistically significant.
(iii) Impossible to tell from the results above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Statistically significant.

This is tested in the following line:
        
```
                           Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
other:(Intercept)         -1.168143   0.388183 -3.0093 0.002619 **
```

:::
        
### Part (d)

The probability that a two-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat invertebrates
and the probability that a two-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat other food.


(i) Statistically significant.
(ii) Not statistically significant.
(iii) Impossible to tell from the results above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible to tell.

This difference is not explicitly tested
in the output above,
since fish is the reference category.

:::

### Part (e)

The odds that a three-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat fish
and the odds that a three-meter-long alligator
will primarily eat invertebrates.


(i) Statistically significant.
(ii) Not statistically significant.
(iii) Impossible to tell from the results above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible to tell.

This analysis does not use odds.

:::

## Problem 4

(5 points)
Which of the following models could be applied to these data?
Select all that apply.


(a) The cumulative logits model, which assumes that for each $m\in\{0,1,2,\dotsc,M-1\}$,
$$
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i \le m \middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i > m \middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip} \text{.}
$$
(b) The proportional odds model, which assumes that for each $m\in\{0,1,2,\dotsc,M-1\}$,
$$
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i \le m \middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i > m \middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p} X_{ip} \text{.}
$$
(c) The adjacent categories model, which assumes that for each $m\in\{1,2,\dotsc,M\}$,
$$
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i = m\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i = m - 1\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip} \text{.}
$$
(d) The restricted adjacent categories model, which assumes that for each $m\in\{1,2,\dotsc,M\}$,
$$
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i = m\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i = m - 1\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p} X_{ip} \text{.}
$$
(e) None of the above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

None of the above.
All of these models require the outcome to have ordered levels.
There's no natural ordering to fish, invertebrates, and other.

:::
